evidence.title: Trachilos (Western Crete, Greece) [Strongly Contested]: ~5.7–6.05 Ma trackways
evidence.dateBasis: Foraminiferal biostratigraphy beneath Messinian evaporites
evidence.summary: Over 50 carbonate shoreline trackways near Kissamos described by Gierliński et al. (2017) with adducted hallux and plantar ball impressions interpreted by the authors as hominin-like. How it got there: During the Messinian Salinity Crisis (~6.0–5.3 Ma), sea-level drops and landbridges linked Greece, Anatolia, and North Africa.
evidence.limits: Strongly contested: most paleoanthropologists question hominin attribution (potentially convergent primate or bear/mammal print or taphonomic erosion); listed for completeness alongside African Miocene anchors.

evidence.title: Gona Western Margin As Duma (Afar, Ethiopia): 4.51–4.32 Ma Ardipithecus ramidus
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar tuff correlation & paleomagnetism
evidence.summary: Jaws, teeth, and foot phalanges of Ardipithecus ramidus from As Duma along the Afar Rift scarp ~75 km north of Aramis. How they got there: Autochthonous Afar woodland/riparian rift-valley lineage evolving from late Miocene Ethiopian Ardipithecus kadabba.
evidence.limits: Isolated partial elements compared with the Aramis AR2 partial skeleton.

evidence.title: Dikika DIK-55 (Afar, Ethiopia) [Contested Cutmarks]: 3.39 Ma modified bone
evidence.dateBasis: Stratified beneath 3.24 Ma Sidi Hakoma Tuff
evidence.summary: Bovid rib and femur shaft bearing linear V-shaped grooves and percussion fractures reported by McPherron et al. (2010) as stone-tool cutmarks possibly made by Australopithecus afarensis prior to Oldowan tools. How they got there: Local Afar Australopithecus foraging along floodplain channels.
evidence.limits: Taphonomic critics argue coarse-sand trampling or crocodile bite marks mimic stone-tool grooves; no in situ stone tools were found in the bed.

evidence.title: Omo Shungura Member F (Omo 57 & 123, Ethiopia): 2.34 Ma quartz Oldowan
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar dating of Tuff F (2.32 Ma)
evidence.summary: Tiny sharp quartz flakes and bipolar cores stratified above Tuff F in the Lower Omo Valley where Paranthropus aethiopicus and early Homo coexisted. How they got there: Riparian Omo–Turkana corridor hominin toolmaking.
evidence.limits: Both early Homo and Paranthropus appear in Member F strata; neither taxon is uniquely proven as sole knapper.

evidence.title: Senga 5A (Upper Semliki, DR Congo) [Age Debated]: ~2.3–2.0 Ma Western Rift Oldowan
evidence.dateBasis: Lusso Beds molluscan & mammalian biostratigraphy
evidence.summary: Quartz Oldowan flakes and choppers recovered from the Lusso Beds in the Albertine/Western Rift along Lake Edward. How they got there: Forest-savanna mosaic corridor linking Lake Victoria/Rift Valley westward into Congo Basin headwaters.
evidence.limits: Geoarchaeological debate over whether younger artifacts intruded or washed onto Pliocene fossil surfaces.

evidence.title: Fejej FJ-1 (South Omo, Ethiopia): 1.96 Ma dense Oldowan living floor
evidence.dateBasis: Magnetostratigraphy (Olduvai Subchron) & 40Ar/39Ar tephra
evidence.summary: In situ quartz and basalt Oldowan workshop and animal-processing camp excavated near the Ethiopian–Kenyan Turkana border. How they got there: Local East African Rift Oldowan adaptation.
evidence.limits: Taxonomic attribution of the FJ-1 toolmaker (H. habilis vs early H. erectus) is inferred from contemporaneous Turkana fossils.

evidence.title: Koobi Fora Area 123 & FxJj 1/3/50 (East Turkana, Kenya): 1.9–1.5 Ma H. habilis & Oldowan
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar KBS Tuff (1.87 Ma) & Okote Tuff complex
evidence.summary: KBS-Member Homo habilis cranium KNM-ER 1813 (~1.9–1.8 Ma, ~510 cc brain) alongside refitted Oldowan butchery sites FxJj 1, FxJj 3, and FxJj 50. How they got there: Indigenous radiation of diverse early Homo across paleo-Lake Turkana floodplains.
evidence.limits: Persistent morphological gap between small-brained KNM-ER 1813 (H. habilis) and large-brained KNM-ER 1470 (H. rudolfensis).

evidence.title: Koobi Fora Area 104 & 130 (Kenya): 1.78–1.55 Ma Homo erectus (KNM-ER 3733) & P. boisei
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar Lorenyang / Okote Tuff tephrochronology
evidence.summary: Landmark early African Homo erectus cranium KNM-ER 3733 (~1.78 Ma, ~848 cc) found in stratigraphic contemporaneity with Paranthropus boisei cranium KNM-ER 406, demonstrating niche partitioning. How they got there: East African Rift center of early H. erectus dispersal.
evidence.limits: Dating of isolated crania relies on local tuff correlation across faulted Area 104/130 outcrops.

evidence.title: Ileret FwJj14E (East Turkana, Kenya): 1.52 Ma Homo erectus & P. boisei trackways
evidence.dateBasis: Okote / Lower Ileret Tuff 40Ar/39Ar dating (~1.52 Ma)
evidence.summary: Dozens of modern-striding Homo erectus footprints (Bennett et al. 2009) plus 2024 Science confirmation (Hatala et al. 2024) that a distinct Paranthropus boisei gait crossed the very same lakeshore mud flat within hours or days of H. erectus. How they got there: Sympatric wetland foraging by two distinct hominin genera.
evidence.limits: Two separate species track-makers inferred quantitatively from hallux adduction and arch biomechanics.

evidence.title: Melka Kunture Gombore I & Garba XII (Ethiopian Highlands): 1.7–1.5 Ma H. erectus at 2,000 m
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar Upper Awash tuffs & magnetostratigraphy
evidence.summary: Gombore I Oldowan camp with Homo erectus humerus (1.6 Ma) and Garba XII early-to-Acheulean levels on the cool 2,000 m Ethiopian plateau (Mussi et al. 2023 Science). How they got there: Cold/hypoxic highland adaptation along the Upper Awash headwaters.
evidence.limits: Volcanic alluvial reworking requires fine stratigraphic micro-excavation between ash units.

evidence.title: Olduvai Gorge Lower Bed II FLK West (Tanzania): 1.70 Ma earliest Olduvai Acheulean
evidence.dateBasis: Tuff IIA / Fluvial Lower Bed II stratigraphy
evidence.summary: Rich assemblage of large Acheulean handaxes and cleavers alongside butchered megafauna (Díez-Martín et al. 2015), contemporaneous with Turkana Kokiselei 4. How they got there: Technological innovation among early Homo erectus in East Africa.
evidence.limits: Direct skeletal remains of the handaxe makers are sparse within FLK West Trench 1.

evidence.title: Olduvai Gorge LLK Upper Bed II (OH 9, Tanzania): ~1.4 Ma large Homo erectus calvaria
evidence.dateBasis: Upper Bed II Tuff IID stratigraphy
evidence.summary: Thick-browed, ~1,067 cc adult Homo erectus braincase ('Chellean Man' OH 9) excavated by Louis Leakey in 1960 in association with classic Acheulean large cutting tools. How they got there: Evolved African H. erectus population at Serengeti/Olduvai paleolake.
evidence.limits: Single surface-eroded calvaria lacking face and postcrania.

evidence.title: Peninj (West Lake Natron, Tanzania): ~1.5 Ma Paranthropus boisei & early Acheulean
evidence.dateBasis: Humbu Formation basalt/tuff K-Ar & 40Ar/39Ar dating
evidence.summary: Robust P. boisei mandible (Peninj 1, 1964) and lakeside RHS-Mugulud / MHS-Bayasi Acheulean handaxe sites preserving phytolith traces of acacia woodworking. How they got there: Gregory Rift lake chain connecting Olduvai, Natron, and Olorgesailie.
evidence.limits: P. boisei mandible and nearby Acheulean quarry floors belong to sympatric lineages.

evidence.title: Chesowanja (Baringo Basin, Kenya): ~1.42 Ma P. boisei & baked-clay fire debate
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar & paleomagnetic basalt dating in Chemoigut Formation
evidence.summary: Crushed P. boisei cranium (KNM-CH 1 / CH 304) and Oldowan/Developed Oldowan tools clustered around thermally altered (~400°C) burnt clay lumps reported by Gowlett et al. (1981). How they got there: Central Kenya Rift alluvial fan.
evidence.limits: Whether baked clay reflects controlled hominin campfires or smoldering wild tree-stump fires remains debated.

evidence.title: Konso-Gardula KGA10-525 (Ethiopia): 1.43 Ma Paranthropus boisei cranium & Acheulean
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar Tuff T-2 (1.43 Ma)
evidence.summary: Well-preserved adult male Paranthropus boisei cranium and mandible (KGA10-525) alongside earliest Homo erectus mandibles and Acheulean bifaces in southern Ethiopia. How they got there: Southern Ethiopian Rift lake basin corridor linking Omo and Afar.
evidence.limits: Rich Acheulean bifaces were mostly made by sympatric H. erectus rather than P. boisei.

evidence.title: Gadeb Plain (Bale Highlands, Ethiopia): 1.45–1.0 Ma Acheulean at 2,300–2,400 m
evidence.dateBasis: Magnetostratigraphy & pumice tephra correlation (~1.45 Ma base)
evidence.summary: Basalt and welded-ignimbrite Acheulean handaxes, cleavers, and burnt rocks on the cool Bale paleolake plain (de la Torre 2011), proving early Homo mastered high-altitude cold plateau habitats. How they got there: Ascended Rift escarpment along Webi Shebele tributaries.
evidence.limits: Lacks direct hominin skeletal fossils; toolmaker inferred as Homo erectus.

evidence.title: Nyabusosi NY 18 (Toro-Semliki, Western Uganda): ~1.5 Ma Western Rift Oldowan
evidence.dateBasis: Behanga Tuff (~1.5 Ma) & Oluka/Nyakabingo biochronology
evidence.summary: In situ quartz Oldowan cores and flakes stratified in Albertine Rift lakebeds north of the Rwenzori Mountains. How they got there: Dispersal from Eastern Rift into tropical Albertine forest-savanna ecotone.
evidence.limits: No associated hominin bones preserved in acidic Western Rift silts.

evidence.title: Olorgesailie Member 1–7 (Southern Kenya Rift): 1.2–0.99 Ma massive Acheulean handaxes
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar pumice & volcanic ash dating across Members 1–7
evidence.summary: Dense carpets of hundreds of volcanic-lava Acheulean handaxes (Member 1 dated ~992 ka) paired with Theropithecus oswaldi baboon and hippo butchery. How they got there: Thriving seasonal Rift paleolake corridor connecting Magadi, Natron, and Central Kenya.
evidence.limits: Later KNM-OG 45500 hominin frontal (~900 ka) postdates Member 1 slightly.

evidence.title: Engel Ela & Mulhuli-Amo (Danakil Depression, Eritrea): ~1.0 Ma Red Sea corridor H. erectus
evidence.dateBasis: Jaramillo Subchron (1.07–0.99 Ma) magnetostratigraphy & fission-track
evidence.summary: UA 31 cranium/pelvis (Buia) and nearby Mulhuli-Amo parietal/occipital bones with Acheulean handaxes directly overlooking the Red Sea coastal margin of Eritrea. How they got there: Northern Afar–Danakil pathway adjacent to both Bab el-Mandeb and Nile corridors out of Africa.
evidence.limits: Morphology blends classic African H. erectus traits with derived supraorbital/parietal breadth.

evidence.title: Gondolin GD 2 (North West, South Africa): ~1.8 Ma Paranthropus robustus
evidence.dateBasis: Paleomagnetism & bovid biochronology
evidence.summary: In situ megadont mandibular molar GDA-2 establishing Paranthropus robustus presence northeast of Sterkfontein during Olduvai Subchron warming/drying cycles. How they got there: Southern African Highveld dolomitic spring/karst refugium.
evidence.limits: Lacks stone tools; small hominin fossil count from GD 2 breccia.

evidence.title: Rietputs 15 (Vaal River, Northern Cape, South Africa): 1.7–1.3 Ma cosmogenic earliest S. African Acheulean
evidence.dateBasis: Isochron 26Al/10Be cosmogenic nuclide burial dating of alluvial gravel diamonds pits
evidence.summary: Hornfels/andesite Acheulean handaxes and cleavers buried in deep Vaal River diamond-bearing gravels dated cosmogenically by Gibbon et al. (2009), proving Acheulean handaxe makers reached South Africa rapidly after East African origins. How they got there: Riverine savanna/Highveld corridor along interior Orange-Vaal drainages.
evidence.limits: Alluvial terrace gravels lack preserved hominin bone; artifacts mildly rolled.

evidence.title: Zarqa Valley / Dawqara Formation (Jordan): 2.48–1.95 Ma earliest Levant Oldowan
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar basalt, paleomagnetism (Matuyama-Olduvai) & mammalian biochronology (Scardia et al. 2019)
evidence.summary: Core-and-flake chert Oldowan artifacts and cut-marked Mammuthus meridionalis fauna in fluvial terraces along the Zarqa River (Scardia et al. 2019), pushing hominin presence at Asia's western threshold earlier than Dmanisi. How they got there: Overland via Sinai–Jordan Rift Valley during Late Pliocene humid 'Green Sahara/Arabia' intervals.
evidence.limits: Debated whether earliest Zone 1 conglomerates span 2.48 Ma or cluster closer to ~2.0–1.95 Ma; no skeletal fossils preserved yet.

evidence.title: Erq el-Ahmar (Central Jordan Valley, Israel): ~1.96–1.78 Ma Olduvai-subchron Oldowan
evidence.dateBasis: Olduvai Normal Magnetochron (Ron & Levi 2001) & tephra/fauna
evidence.summary: Flint core-choppers and flakes in paleolake Erq el-Ahmar beds spanning the Olduvai magnetic polarity subchron just south of the Sea of Galilee. How they got there: Northward along the Dead Sea–Jordan Rift Valley freshwater corridor from Sinai.
evidence.limits: Small lithic sample; ongoing discussion over exact correlation of artifact horizon to dated magnetic cores.

evidence.title: ʿUbeidiya UB 10749 (Jordan Valley, Israel): ~1.5 Ma large-bodied Homo erectus vertebra
evidence.dateBasis: Biostratigraphy & paleomagnetism in Fi/II-23 Acheulean layers
evidence.summary: Juvenile lumbar vertebra UB 10749 analyzed by Barash et al. (2022) proving a distinct Out-of-Africa dispersal of large-bodied East African-grade Homo erectus carrying Early Acheulean handaxes through the Levant ~300 kyr after small-bodied Dmanisi hominins. How they got there: Second Out-of-Africa II Rift dispersal wave.
evidence.limits: Single vertebral specimen from museum re-study; complements rich Acheulean lithic strata.

evidence.title: Bizat Ruhama (Northern Negev, Israel): 1.6–1.2 Ma small-flake Mode 1 on arid fringe
evidence.dateBasis: Reverse Matuyama paleomagnetism, ESR & red hamra soil stratigraphy
evidence.summary: Expedient bipolar small-chert flake workshop beside seasonal wetlands in the semiarid Negev coastal plain (Zaidner 2013), showing early Eurasian hominins succeeded outside Rift lakes using Mode 1 minimalism rather than handaxes. How they got there: Coastal Levant–Sinai plain north from Africa.
evidence.limits: No hominin skeletal fossils recovered; broad Early Pleistocene age bracket.

evidence.title: Kermek, Bogatyri & Rodniki 1 (Taman Peninsula, Sea of Azov, Russia): ~2.1–1.2 Ma Tamanian Oldowan [Debated]
evidence.dateBasis: Psekups/Tamanian mammalian biochronology, magnetostratigraphy & marine stratigraphy
evidence.summary: Dolomite choppers, picks, and flakes associated with southern mammoth/elasmothere bones in Azov coastal lagoon beds reported by Shchelinsky et al. If confirmed, they document the earliest northern Black Sea steppe corridor (~2.1–1.8 Ma at Kermek; ~1.6–1.2 Ma at Bogatyri/Sinyaya Balka). How they got there: Northward from Transcaucasia/Dmanisi along Black Sea or Caspian littoral corridors.
evidence.limits: Geoarchaeological critics debate natural high-energy wave-fracturing (geofacts) vs intentional knapping and caution on secondary marine re-deposition.

evidence.title: Muhkai II & Ainikab 1 (Central Dagestan, North Caucasus, Russia): ~2.0–1.5 Ma [Debated]
evidence.dateBasis: Akchagylian–Apsheronian palynology & Matuyama paleomagnetism
evidence.summary: Over 30 stacked flint-bearing horizons at 1,600 m in Dagestan (Muhkai II, Ainikab 1–2, Gegalashur) excavated by Amirkhanov et al., proposing a major Early Pleistocene route east of the Greater Caucasus along the paleo-Caspian western shelf. How they got there: Circum-Caspian lowland corridor northward from Georgia/Azerbaijan.
evidence.limits: Magnetostratigraphy and raw flint frost/slope fracturing vs anthropogenic knapping remain actively scrutinized outside Russia.

evidence.title: Kocabaş (Denizli Basin, SW Turkey): ~1.6–1.2 Ma Homo erectus calvaria
evidence.dateBasis: 26Al/10Be cosmogenic nuclides (~1.6–1.2 Ma) & Matuyama paleomagnetism (Lebatard 2014)
evidence.summary: Partial Homo erectus braincase preserved in commercial travertine blocks in southwestern Anatolia (Lebatard et al. 2014), preserving morphological affinities with African KNM-ER 3733 / OH 9 and Asian Zhoukoudian as well as possible tuberculosis-like endocranial lesions. How they got there: Anatolian landbridge connecting the Levantine corridor across Turkey toward Greece and the Balkans.
evidence.limits: Recovered during quarry sawing without micro-contextual stone tools in direct contact.

evidence.title: Gediz River / Kula (Manisa, Western Anatolia, Turkey): 1.24–1.17 Ma basalt-dated flake
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar dating of capping & meandering river-terrace basalts (Maddy et al. 2015)
evidence.summary: In situ struck quartzite flake discovered stratified directly beneath precisely 40Ar/39Ar-dated basalt lava terraces along the Gediz River (Maddy et al. 2015), providing an unimpeachably dated anchor on the Aegean gateway into Europe. How they got there: Westward river-terrace dispersal across Anatolia toward Thrace and the Aegean.
evidence.limits: Single diagnostic artifact recovered directly within the basalt-bracketed river gravel.

evidence.title: Dursunlu (Konya Basin, Central Anatolia, Turkey): ~1.0–0.9 Ma quartz artifacts
evidence.dateBasis: Reverse Matuyama / Late Villafranchian-Galerian biochronology in lignite quarry
evidence.summary: Quartz core-and-flake assemblage and butchered wetland mammals recovered deep within Central Anatolian lignite seams (Güleç et al. 1999). How they got there: Across Central Anatolian lake basins connecting Taurus foothills to western Turkey.
evidence.limits: Chronology rests on biochronological vole/mammal correlation and Matuyama polarity prior to Jaramillo-Brunhes shifts.

evidence.title: Grăunceanu (Olteț River Valley, Romania): ~1.95 Ma cut-marked Villafranchian bones
evidence.dateBasis: High-precision U-Pb & biochronology of 4,500+ Villafranchian fossils (Curran et al. 2025)
evidence.summary: Curran et al. (2025, Nature Communications) identified statistically diagnostic, high-confidence hominin stone-tool cut marks across multiple fossil mammal bones at Grăunceanu in southern Romania ~1.95 Ma—pushing Eurasian/European hominin arrival ~180 kyr earlier than Dmanisi! How they got there: East-to-west savanna-steppe corridor skirting north or west of the Black Sea / Lower Danube.
evidence.limits: Stone tools were not recovered during the 1960s paleontological dig; attribution relies on blind quantitative 3D confocal microscopy of cutmarks.

evidence.title: Kozarnika Cave (NW Bulgaria): 1.6–1.4 Ma Lower Danube Mode 1 & engraved bone claim
evidence.dateBasis: Mimomys pusillus vole biochronology & magnetostratigraphy in Basal Level 13
evidence.summary: Deep Danubian limestone cave containing >1,500 flint Mode 1 flakes, cores, and disputed intentionally incised animal bone in its oldest Level 13 (~1.6–1.4 Ma), anchoring the Balkan gateway from Anatolia toward Central Europe and Korolevo. How they got there: Crossing Bosphorus/Thrace lowland bridges during Early Pleistocene low sea stands.
evidence.limits: Small-mammal biochronological dating of Basal Level 13 has not yet been supplemented by cosmogenic nuclides.

evidence.title: Lézignan-la-Cèbe / Bois-de-Riquet (Hérault, Southern France): ~1.57–1.2 Ma basalt-dated Oldowan
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar capping basalt (1.57 Ma) & Villafranchian fauna
evidence.summary: Basalt and quartz Mode 1 artifacts alongside >20 Late Villafranchian mammal species at Bois-de-Riquet / Lézignan-la-Cèbe in Mediterranean France (Crochet et al. 2009). How they got there: Northern Mediterranean coastal plains corridor from Italy or via Rhône–Languedoc.
evidence.limits: US-2 hominin artifacts may be slightly younger (~1.2 Ma) than the 1.57 Ma US-1 volcanic tuff bed.

evidence.title: Pirro Nord P13 (Gargano Peninsula, Apulia, Italy): 1.6–1.3 Ma Mediterranean Mode 1
evidence.dateBasis: Pirro Faunal Unit (Late Villafranchian, pre-Jaramillo)
evidence.summary: Over 340 bipolar/centripetal flint artifacts inside fissure P13 along the Gargano paleoisland/peninsula alongside giant geladas (Theropithecus), sabertooths, and African-derived fauna (Rook & Martínez-Navarro 2013). How they got there: Exposed Po Valley / circum-Adriatic land corridors from the Balkans during Pleistocene glacial lowstands.
evidence.limits: Fissure-fill karst context relies on mammalian biochronology rather than radiometric ashes.

evidence.title: Fuente Nueva-3 (Orce, Guadix-Baza Basin, Spain): ~1.3–1.2 Ma mammoth butchery & Oldowan
evidence.dateBasis: ESR, paleomagnetism & Mimomys savini rodent biochronology
evidence.summary: Limestone hammerstones and flint Mode 1 flakes clustered directly around a Mammuthus meridionalis carcass scavenged competitively with giant hyenas (Pachycrocuta brevirostris), complementing Barranco León's BL-0 molar. How they got there: East-to-west peri-Mediterranean / Pyrenean dispersal across southern Iberia; Gibraltar crossing lacks confirmed Pliocene/Early Pleistocene support.
evidence.limits: Radiometric/ESR age uncertainties place Orce between ~1.4 and ~1.2 Ma.

evidence.title: Sima del Elefante TE7 (Atapuerca, Spain): 1.4–1.1 Ma ATE7-1 ('Pink') H. aff. erectus face
evidence.dateBasis: Cosmogenic 26Al/10Be, paleomagnetism (Matuyama) & biostratigraphy (Huguet 2025)
evidence.summary: Recovered in Level TE7 beneath the 1.2 Ma TE9c mandible, the ATE7-1 adult left maxilla and zygomatic ('Pink', Huguet et al. 2025 Nature) is the oldest human facial fossil in Western Europe—more primitive than H. antecessor and assigned to Homo aff. erectus. How they got there: Across southern Europe into the Duero–Ebro watershed corridor during warm interglacials.
evidence.limits: Severe Early Pleistocene cooling events (~1.12 Ma, Margari 2023 Science) subsequently depopulated Iberia until later pulses.

evidence.title: Grotte du Vallonnet (Roquebrune-Cap-Martin, SE France): 1.2–1.1 Ma U-Pb cave tools
evidence.dateBasis: U-Pb flowstone stalagmite dating (~1.2 Ma) & ESR/paleomagnetism (Michel 2017)
evidence.summary: Coastal Ligurian limestone cave sealed beneath U-Pb-dated stalagmites (~1.22–1.13 Ma, Michel et al. 2017) containing limestone/quartzite choppers, flakes, and cut-marked deer/bovid bones. How they got there: Narrow Ligurian-Provençal coastal corridor linking northern Italy to southern France.
evidence.limits: Modest artifact assemblage (~100 pieces); debate over minor marine beach-cobble component.

evidence.title: Pont-de-Lavaud & Lunery (Loire Valley / Berry, Central France): ~1.1–1.05 Ma quartz Mode 1
evidence.dateBasis: ESR quartz-bleaching dating of Creuse & Cher fluvial terraces (Despriée 2006/2018)
evidence.summary: Northwesternmost confirmed pre-1 Ma sites in Europe (~47°N), yielding >8,000 bipolar quartz Mode 1 pieces on high Creuse and Cher river terraces (Despriée et al. 2006, 2018). How they got there: Northward along Atlantic–Rhône–Loire river valleys into northern Europe during mild MIS 31/29 interglacials.
evidence.limits: No hominin skeletal remains preserved in acidic Loire quartz gravels.

evidence.title: Untermaßfeld (Thuringia, Germany) [Disputed]: ~1.05 Ma northern Europe claim
evidence.dateLabel: ~1.05 million years ago (anthropic claim strongly disputed)
evidence.dateBasis: Jaramillo Magnetosubchron & Epivillafranchian Werra River floodplain
evidence.summary: Exceptionally rich Werra River floodplain bonebed (~1.05 Ma) where García et al. argued for rare stone tools and hominin cutmarks. If verified, it would mark >50°N Early Pleistocene hominin arrival across Central Europe. How they got there: Rhine–Danube–Werra river corridors during Jaramillo warmth.
evidence.limits: Excavation director R.-D. Kahlke and geoarchaeologists strongly dispute all lithics/cutmarks as river-ice or carnivore pseudotools.

evidence.title: Ca' Belvedere di Monte Poggiolo (Emilia-Romagna, Italy): ~1.0–0.85 Ma Mode 1 flint
evidence.dateBasis: ESR, paleomagnetism (Matuyama) & coastal Adriatic delta cycles (Muttoni 2018)
evidence.summary: Over 4,000 exceptionally sharp refitting flint flakes and unidirectional cores deposited in paleo-coastal gravels during northern Adriatic Po Plain lowstands. How they got there: Early Galerian wave across the exposed Adriatic plain from the Balkans.
evidence.limits: Debate persists over whether age sits right before the ~0.99 Ma Jaramillo top or slightly later (~0.85 Ma) prior to the Brunhes boundary.

evidence.title: Barranc de la Boella (Tarragona, Spain): ~1.0–0.8 Ma earliest European Acheulean
evidence.dateBasis: Cosmogenic nuclides, ESR & Matuyama magnetostratigraphy (Vallverdú 2014; Ollé 2023)
evidence.summary: Large Acheulean schist picks and crude cleavers alongside a butchered Mammuthus meridionalis skeleton on an ancient Francolí delta (Vallverdú et al. 2014; Ollé et al. 2023)—Europe's oldest large-cutting-tool technology. How they got there: Fresh dispersal from Africa/Levant or Southwest Asia after Early Pleistocene Acheulean emergence.
evidence.limits: Span across the Matuyama-Jaramillo transition permits dates between ~1.0 Ma and ~0.8 Ma.

evidence.title: Masol (Siwalik Frontal Range, Punjab, NW India) [Contested]: ~2.6 Ma Pliocene claim
evidence.dateBasis: Gauss-Matuyama paleomagnetism & Quranwala Zone Siwalik stratigraphy (Cauche 2021)
evidence.summary: Chopper-cores and purported cut-marked bovid/equid bones reported by Dambricourt Malassé and Cauche (2016, 2021) in 2.6 Ma sub-Himalayan Siwalik silts. How they got there (if confirmed): Late Pliocene northern Indo-Gangetic piedmont dispersal east from Africa/Southwest Asia.
evidence.limits: Strongly contested by most South Asian paleoanthropologists, who question whether quartz cobbles and bone grooves weathered out in situ from 2.6 Ma silts or derived from younger Pleistocene river terraces.

evidence.title: Pabbi Hills (Punjab, Northern Pakistan): ~2.2–1.2 Ma Potwar Early Pleistocene artifacts
evidence.dateBasis: Matuyama-Olduvai-Jaramillo paleomagnetism across >1,000 m Siwalik anticline
evidence.summary: Surface and sandstone-horizon Mode 1 flakes and choppers eroding from well-dated Early Pleistocene fluvial sands along the Jhelum margin (Rendell & Dennell 1989). How they got there: Iranian–Makran–Indus piedmont lowland corridor from West Asia.
evidence.limits: Surface artifacts lack dense living-floor clustering and no hominin bone has been recovered.

evidence.title: Morgaon & Bori (Deccan Basalt, Maharashtra, India) [Age Debated]: ~1.4–0.8 Ma early Indian Acheulean
evidence.dateBasis: Matuyama reverse polarity & debated volcanic ash Ar-Ar correlations
evidence.summary: In situ basalt-flake Acheulean cleavers and handaxes buried below reverse-polarity alluvial clays on the Karha and Kukdi rivers alongside Attirampakkam (1.5 Ma) and Isampur (1.2 Ma). How they got there: Interior Indian peninsula savanna-river valleys east from the Indus gateway.
evidence.limits: YTT-like (74 ka) vs Early Pleistocene reworked tephra dates remain actively debated at Bori.

evidence.title: Xihoudu (Ruicheng, Shanxi, China): 2.43 Ma (26Al/10Be) vs 1.27 Ma northern China artifacts
evidence.dateBasis: Isochron 26Al/10Be burial dating (Shen 2020) vs Yellow River paleomagnetic section (Zhu 2003)
evidence.summary: Flaked quartzite cores, scrapers, and burnt deer antlers in cross-bedded Yellow River sands. Shen et al.'s (2020) isochron 26Al/10Be age of 2.43 ± 0.06 Ma would surpass Shangchen as East Asia's oldest archaeological site. How they got there: Mid-latitude Eurasian steppe–loess belt along the Yellow River Bend.
evidence.limits: Wide gap between earlier paleomagnetic age (~1.27 Ma) and new cosmogenic burial age (~2.43 Ma) remains unresolved.

evidence.title: Longgupo Cave (Wushan, Three Gorges, China) [Taxon Debated]: ~2.48–2.0 Ma mandible & tools
evidence.dateBasis: Coupled ESR/U-series (Han 2022) & magnetostratigraphy (Sun 2022)
evidence.summary: Deep Three Gorges karst fissure yielding stone cobble artifacts and the famous Longgupo mandible fragment with P4–M1 alongside Gigantopithecus fauna. How they got there: South Asian / subtropical Yangtze river corridors south of the Qinling Mountains.
evidence.limits: Taxonomic identity of the Longgupo mandible is heavily debated between early Homo/hominin and an extinct Miocene-relict Asian ape (Lufengpithecus-like), though lithic artifacts in upper levels are widely accepted.

evidence.title: Renzidong Cave (Fanchang, Anhui, China) [Disputed]: ~2.2–2.0 Ma Early Pleistocene claim
evidence.dateBasis: Early Pleistocene mammalian biochronology (Homoctenomys/Ailuropoda microta)
evidence.summary: Vertical karst fissure near the Lower Yangtze yielding >60 chert/bone items interpreted by Chinese excavators as early Mode 1 artifacts alongside cold-and-warm Early Pleistocene mammals. How they got there: Subtropical Lower Yangtze corridor.
evidence.limits: No hominin fossils; many researchers question whether fractured chert/bone reflects natural karst collapse rather than knapping.

evidence.title: Longgudong Cave (Jianshi, Hubei, China): ~2.15–1.8 Ma isolated teeth & lithics
evidence.dateBasis: Paleomagnetism & ESR tooth enamel dating (Li et al. 2017)
evidence.summary: Three isolated bunodont/hominin-like molars (PA 1277–1279) and stone flakes from southwestern Hubei stratified with Stegodon-Ailuropoda fauna. How they got there: Subtropical Three Gorges–Yangtze forested valleys.
evidence.limits: Isolated teeth spark ongoing taxonomic debate between early Homo, Homo erectus, and fossil orangutan (Pongo).

evidence.title: Gongwangling (Lantian, Shaanxi, China): 1.63 Ma Homo erectus cranium
evidence.dateBasis: Loess–paleosol L22–S22 magnetostratigraphic revision (Zhu et al. 2015)
evidence.summary: Thick-walled partial adult calvaria (~780 cc) and maxilla/teeth revised by Zhu et al. (2015) and Pan et al. (2022) from ~1.15 Ma back to ~1.63 Ma on the Qinling foothills—just 20 km from 2.12 Ma Shangchen! How they got there: Loess Plateau–Qinling north slope dispersal via Hexi Corridor and Eurasian steppes.
evidence.limits: Slightly distorted vault and associated subtropical/warm fauna indicating humid interglacial survival.

evidence.title: Xiaochangliang (Nihewan Basin, Hebei, China): 1.36 Ma northern 40°N lake camp
evidence.dateBasis: High-resolution Nihewan paleolake magnetostratigraphy (Zhu / Yang 2016)
evidence.summary: Landmark >3,000-artifact small-chert bipolar Mode 1 assemblage showing sustained hominin survival near 40°N despite harsh winter-monsoon seasonality. How they got there: Northeastward dispersal across North China plain lake basins from Loess Plateau.
evidence.limits: No skeletal hominin remains recovered in Nihewan fluvio-lacustrine silts.

evidence.title: Banshan (1.32 Ma) & Feiliang (1.2 Ma), Nihewan Basin (Hebei, China): refitted lakeshore knapping
evidence.dateBasis: Nihewan Basin magnetostratigraphy (Ao 2013; Pei 2017)
evidence.summary: Successive fine-grained lakeshore horizons with high artifact-refitting sets proving systematic local chert procurement and short-term carcass processing across seasonal paleolake fluctuations. How they got there: Long-term multi-century residency in the Nihewan paleolake refugium.
evidence.limits: Lithic-only assemblages; seasonality constraints remain modeled from pollen/faunal teeth.

evidence.title: Cenjiawan & Donggutuo (Nihewan Basin, Hebei, China): 1.1 Ma earliest Eurasian prepared cores
evidence.dateBasis: Pre-Jaramillo Matuyama magnetostratigraphy (Ma et al. 2024 PNAS)
evidence.summary: 3D technological refitting at Cenjiawan (~1.1 Ma, Ma et al. 2024 PNAS) uncovered predetermined core-preparation strategies ~300 kyr before Europe/Africa, demonstrating unexpected East Asian cognitive sophistication in Homo erectus. How they got there: Locally evolved technological innovation within northern Chinese H. erectus populations.
evidence.limits: Lithic refits without associated human skulls; Donggutuo wedges (~1.1 Ma) show parallel platform-rotation skill.

evidence.title: Trinil (Solo River, East Java, Indonesia): ~1.0–0.5 Ma Homo erectus holotype & engraved shell
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar & luminescence dating of Main Bonebed / Trinil HK (Joordens 2015)
evidence.summary: Eugène Dubois's 1891 discovery of the holotype Homo erectus skullcap (Trinil 2) and femur, plus Joordens et al.'s (2015) zigzag-engraved freshwater Pseudodon mussel shell. How they got there: Walked overland south across the exposed Sunda Shelf landbridge during glacial low sea levels (~100+ m drops linking Malaya, Sumatra, Borneo, and Java).
evidence.limits: Old 1890s Main Bonebed excavation spans ~1.0 Ma to ~0.43 Ma reworked volcanic lahar deposits; earlier ~1.5–1.3 Ma Sangiran Pucangan beds anchor arrival.

evidence.title: Calio (Walanae Basin, South Sulawesi, Indonesia): >1.04 Ma earliest Wallacean sea-crossers
evidence.dateBasis: US-ESR Celebochoerus teeth & paleomagnetic reverse polarity (Hakim et al. 2025 Nature)
evidence.summary: Seven sharp-edged chert flakes from fluvial sandstones at Calio (Hakim et al. 2025, Nature) pushed hominin colonization of oceanic Sulawesi past 1.04 Ma—older than Wolo Sege on Flores! How they got there: Required crossing the deep marine Makassar Strait (Wallace's Line, never bridged by land even at lowest sea levels), most likely via accidental storm/tsunami sweepstakes rafting on vegetation mats from Borneo.
evidence.limits: Hominin skeletal fossils have not yet been found in Early Pleistocene Walanae strata to reveal whether islanders resembled H. erectus or already exhibited insular dwarfing.

evidence.title: Cooper's D (Bloubank Valley, Gauteng, South Africa): ~1.5–1.4 Ma P. robustus & bone tools
evidence.dateBasis: U-Pb flowstone dating (~1.53–1.40 Ma, de Ruiter et al. 2009)
evidence.summary: Paranthropus robustus skull COB 101 and teeth alongside Early Pleistocene Oldowan/Early Acheulean stone and termite-digging bone tools. How they got there: Bloubank Valley karst springs and Highveld savanna.
evidence.limits: Bone tools could relate to either P. robustus or sympatric early Homo.

evidence.title: Kilombe & Kariandusi (Central Kenya Rift): ~1.1–0.99 Ma Early Acheulean bifaces
evidence.dateBasis: 40Ar/39Ar volcanic tuff stratigraphy & paleomagnetism (Hoare et al. 2021)
evidence.summary: Hundreds of standardized trachyphonolite and obsidian Acheulean handaxes clustered around extinct Kilombe volcano foothills and Lake Elmenteita shores. How they got there: High-elevation Central Rift valley lakes connecting Olorgesailie and Turkana.
evidence.limits: Lacks associated hominin skeletal fossils; toolmaker attributed to African H. erectus.

evidence.title: Vallparadís (Terrassa, Catalonia, Spain): ~1.0–0.83 Ma late Early Pleistocene Mode 1
evidence.dateBasis: ESR, Matuyama paleomagnetism & paleontological biochronology (Martínez 2010 PNAS)
evidence.summary: Deep lakeside Mode 1 quartz/flint flake sequence alongside butchered hippopotamus and rhinoceros remains in NE Iberia immediately before the Matuyama–Brunhes reversal. How they got there: Mediterranean Catalan gateway along the eastern Pyrenees.
evidence.limits: Combined ESR/magnetostratigraphic revisions bracket peak Layer EVT7 close to ~0.98–0.85 Ma.

evidence.title: Evron Quarry (Western Galilee Coastal Plain, Israel): ~1.0–0.8 Ma Early Acheulean & fire
evidence.dateBasis: Paleomagnetism & micro-spectroscopic FTIR heat-signature analysis (Stepka 2022 PNAS)
evidence.summary: Mediterranean coastal-plain Acheulean bifaces, small flakes, and fauna preserving AI-detected invisible heat-exposure signatures (~500 °C) on flint and bone (Stepka et al. 2022). How they got there: Levantine coastal corridor linking ʿUbeidiya and Eurasian interior.
evidence.limits: Absence of visible hearth ash lenses means heat signatures could involve earliest opportunistic or incipient fire control.

evidence.title: Yiron (Upper Galilee Plateau, Israel) [Strongly Debated]: ~2.4 Ma sub-basalt claim
evidence.dateBasis: K-Ar basalt flow dating reported atop flint gravel horizon (Ronen / de Lumley 2006)
evidence.summary: Claimed flint artifacts eroding beneath a ~2.4 Ma basalt sheet on the Galilee plateau, often cited alongside Zarqa Valley (~2.48–1.95 Ma) in debates over pre-2 Ma Out of Africa I dispersals. How they got there (if confirmed): Levant highland margin north of the Jordan Rift.
evidence.limits: Strongly debated: critics caution small flint sample size and uncertain sub-basalt intrusive context compared with in situ Zarqa excavations.

evidence.title: Ash-Shuwayhitiyah (Al-Jawf, N. Saudi Arabia) [Age Debated]: ~1.3 Ma Arabian Mode 1 claim
evidence.dateBasis: Typological comparison & desert varnish terrace setting (Petraglia 2003)
evidence.summary: Quartzite choppers, polyhedrons, and spheroids discovered along northern Arabian drainage channels (Whalen 1986; Petraglia 2003), frequently invoked for the 'Green Arabia' corridor linking Africa, Levant, and South Asia. How they got there: Monsoonal river/lake activation across the Syrian–Arabian desert interior.
evidence.limits: Surface lag context lacks direct burial OSL/cosmogenic chronology, leaving its true pre-1 Ma vs Middle Pleistocene age unresolved.

waves.title: Late Miocene–Earliest Pliocene African Hominin Distribution
waves.summary: Earliest bipedal/facultatively bipedal hominins spanned forested-to-woodland savannas from Chad (Toros-Menalla) across Kenya (Tugen Hills) to Ethiopia (Middle Awash).
waves.limits: Three discrete fossil pockets separate immense unexcavated central African basins; whether Crete's ~5.7 Ma Trachilos prints reflect Mediterranean Messinian dispersals or non-hominin tracks remains heavily contested.

waves.title: Pan-African Australopithecus & Early Oldowan Spread
waves.summary: Australopiths, Kenyanthropus, and early Paranthropus expanded across Chad, Afar, Turkana, Nyayanga, and South Africa alongside >2.6–3.3 Ma stone-tool origins (Lomekwi, Nyayanga, Namorotukunan, Aïn Boucherit).
waves.limits: North African 2.44 Ma Aïn Boucherit Oldowan implies rapid trans-Saharan Green Sahara crossing well before Out of Africa I in Asia.

waves.title: Out of Africa I Northern Pathway (Sinai–Levant–Caucasus Corridor)
waves.summary: Primary overland exit along the East African Rift–Red Sea escarpment through Sinai into the Jordan Rift (Zarqa 2.48–1.95 Ma, Erq el-Ahmar 1.9 Ma, ʿUbeidiya 1.5 Ma) and north through Anatolia/Mesopotamia to Dmanisi (1.77 Ma).
waves.limits: Both pre-erectus early Homo (~2.4–2.0 Ma) and full-statured H. erectus (~1.5 Ma) appear to have crossed the Levantine corridor in multiple pulses.

waves.title: East-to-West Eurasian Dispersal into Europe (Danube, Carpathians & Mediterranean)
waves.summary: First hominins entered Europe from Southwest Asia/Caucasus rather than Gibraltar—attested at Grăunceanu (~1.95 Ma), Kocabaş (~1.6–1.2 Ma), Kozarnika (1.6–1.4 Ma), Korolevo (1.42 Ma), Pirro Nord, Lézignan, Orce, Sima del Elefante ATE7-1, Vallonnet, and Pont-de-Lavaud.
waves.limits: Severe Early Pleistocene cold spikes (~1.12 Ma) triggered intermittent extirpations across Atlantic Europe before Acheulean re-colonization.

waves.title: Trans-Eurasian Steppe & Monsoon Dispersal to China & South Asia
waves.summary: Savanna and monsoon corridors across Iran, Pakistan (Riwat/Pabbi), India (Attirampakkam, Isampur), and the Eurasian steppe-loess belt brought early Homo / H. erectus to Shangchen (2.12 Ma), Xihoudu, Yuanmou (1.7 Ma), Yunxian (1.77 Ma), Gongwangling (1.63 Ma), and 40°N Nihewan (1.66–1.1 Ma).
waves.limits: Both northern Central Asian steppe routes and southern Indian–Indochina coastal routes may have functioned intermittently during wet/interglacial phases.

waves.title: Sunda Shelf Walk & Open-Sea Wallacean Rafting (Java, Flores & Sulawesi)
waves.summary: Homo erectus walked south across the exposed Sunda Shelf landbridge into Java (~1.5–1.3 Ma Sangiran/Mojokerto), then inadvertently rafted across deep Wallacean ocean currents on storm/tsunami debris mats to reach Sulawesi (>1.04 Ma Calio) and Flores (1.02 Ma Wolo Sege) before 1 million years ago.
waves.limits: Passive/accidental coastal rafting by small founder groups (rather than intentional plank-built navigation) best matches Wallacea's impoverished endemic fauna.

studies.title: Before 1 Million Years Ago: Every Global Hominin & Tool Site (7.0–1.0 Ma)
studies.summary: Complete planetary inventory of 164 known hominin fossil and archaeological localities dated older than 1.0 Ma—spanning Africa, the Levant, Arabia, the Caucasus, Anatolia, Europe, South Asia, China, Sundaland (Java), and Wallacea (Flores & Sulawesi), with species attributions and dispersal hypotheses.
